title: “THOU SHALT NOT KILL”… BUT WHAT IF YOU WEAR A BADGE OR CARRY A RIFLE?
paragraphs: “THOU SHALT NOT KILL”… BUT WHAT IF YOU WEAR A BADGE OR CARRY A RIFLE?
What Scripture actually says about murder, soldiers, police, lethal force, the human heart—and the terrifying responsibility of carrying a weapon while claiming the name of Christ.
There is a particular kind of silence that comes after violence.
Ask the police officer who arrived seconds too late.
Ask the soldier who still remembers the face on the other side of his weapon.
Ask the mother whose son went to war and came home physically alive but somehow quieter.
Ask the Christian who has read the Sixth Commandment a hundred times, then one day looked at the weapon on his belt and wondered:
“If God said, ‘Thou shalt not kill,’ what am I doing?”
Maybe you have never carried a rifle into combat.
Maybe you have never worn a badge.
But stay with me.
Because before this is an article about soldiers and police officers, it is an article about something far closer to all of us.
The human heart.
And Jesus is going to take us somewhere uncomfortable.
The famous words appear in Exodus 20:13. The King James Version renders them:
“Thou shalt not kill.”
But the Hebrew is more precise:
לֹא תִּרְצָח — Lōʾ tirṣāḥ.
Literally, in this commandment, the sense is:
“You shall not murder.”
That distinction matters enormously.

The Hebrew verb comes from רצח — rāṣaḥ, a term associated with unlawful or culpable killing. The commandment is not written as a blanket statement declaring that every circumstance in which one human being causes another human being's death is morally identical.

That becomes evident even within the Torah itself, where the same law given to Israel distinguishes murder from other forms of killing and establishes different consequences according to circumstances and culpability.
So when many modern translations render Exodus 20:13 as “You shall not murder,” they are not weakening God's commandment. They are communicating its meaning more precisely.
And suddenly the question changes.
Not:
“Is every taking of human life murder?”
But:
“When does the taking of human life become murder before God?”
That is a much heavier question.
Because Scripture never treats human life cheaply.
Never.
The person standing across from you—even the criminal, even the enemy, even the person doing terrible evil—is still a human being bearing the dignity God gave humanity.
Genesis 1:27 grounds human worth in something deeper than nationality, uniform, innocence, usefulness, political allegiance, or whether we personally like someone.
Human beings are made in God's image.
That means Christians should never celebrate bloodshed simply because the dead person was called “the enemy.”
There should be no bloodlust in the follower of the Lamb.
No delight in suffering.
No addiction to vengeance.
No fantasy about finally getting permission to hurt someone.
Yet Scripture simultaneously recognizes something painfully obvious about this fallen world:
Sometimes evil must be restrained.
Sometimes innocent people need someone willing to stand between them and the person trying to destroy them.
Imagine the officer responding to a home where a terrified child is screaming.
A violent attacker has a weapon.
The officer has seconds.
Not twenty minutes for theological reflection.
Seconds.
If he does nothing, an innocent person may die.
If he intervenes, the attacker may die.
What does love require in that moment?
That question is much harder than a slogan.
And Scripture does not permit us to solve it by ripping four English words out of Exodus and ignoring everything else God has revealed.
Consider something fascinating in the Gospel of Luke.
Soldiers approached John the Baptist while he was preaching repentance.
They asked:
“And we, what shall we do?”
John could have answered:
“Leave the military immediately.”
But that is not what the text records.
Instead, Luke 3:14 records John warning soldiers against abusing their power—extortion, false accusations, intimidation—and commanding them to be content with their wages.
That detail matters.
John's concern was not merely that these men possessed authority.
His concern was what kind of men they would become while possessing it.
Because power reveals things.
Give a person authority and eventually you discover whether he loves justice...
or merely loves being powerful.
Give someone a weapon and eventually the deeper question becomes unavoidable:
Who is controlling whom?
That is where this becomes intensely personal for every Christian police officer and soldier reading these words.
Your uniform does not suspend your discipleship.
Your badge does not outrank Christ.
Your commanding officer does not become your god.
Your government does not become your savior.
Your weapon does not become your identity.
Before you are an officer...
before you are a soldier...
before you belong to a nation...
if you belong to Jesus Christ,
you belong to Him.
And that means there are things you must never do simply because someone with authority told you to do them.

Scripture's recognition of governing authority is real. Romans 13 describes civil authority as God's servant for good and says that the authority does not “bear the sword in vain,” associating governing authority with the punishment of wrongdoing.
But Romans 13 does not turn governments into gods.
Human authority remains human authority.
When human commands directly contradict God's commands, Acts 5:29 gives the Christian's ultimate allegiance:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.”
So no soldier receives biblical permission to commit atrocities because he was “following orders.”
No police officer receives biblical permission to brutalize someone because that person resisted him.
No government possesses moral authority to transform wickedness into righteousness merely by legalizing it.
And no Christian can hide his conscience behind a uniform.
The weapon may have been issued by the government.
Your soul was not.
It belongs to God.

This is why Christians have wrestled deeply with questions of war, self-defense, policing, capital punishment, conscientious objection, and the use of force throughout church history. Faithful believers have not always reached identical conclusions. Some Christian traditions have embraced pacifism and nonviolence; others have concluded that Scripture permits carefully limited force in defense of the innocent and in legitimate civil authority.
We should be humble enough to acknowledge that history rather than pretending every difficult ethical question can be solved with a meme.
But there is something even more disturbing.
Jesus takes the Sixth Commandment...
and walks straight past the weapon.
Straight past the battlefield.
Straight past the crime scene.
And enters your heart.
In Matthew 5:21–22, Jesus recalls the command against murder and immediately confronts sinful anger and contempt. He exposes the murderous direction of a heart that dehumanizes another person.
One expression appearing in that passage is:
Ῥακά — Rhaka/Raca
an Aramaic expression of contempt.
Do you see what Christ is doing?
We want to ask:
“Jesus, when is killing technically permitted?”
And Jesus looks deeper and asks:
“What is happening inside you toward the person you want to destroy?”
That changes everything.
Because you may never have fired a gun at another human being...
and still carry murder's poison inside your heart.
You can assassinate someone repeatedly in your imagination.
You can hate your father.
Despise your former spouse.
Wish suffering upon your enemy.
Celebrate when someone you hate falls.
You can destroy someone's reputation because you cannot destroy their body.
You can smile in church while secretly wishing another person would disappear.
No blood.
No weapon.
No corpse.
And yet Jesus is exposing the darkness underneath.
Suddenly this article isn't about soldiers anymore, is it?
It's about us.
The police officer must examine his heart.
The soldier must examine his heart.
The civilian must examine his heart.
The pastor must examine his heart.
The person typing furious comments underneath political posts must examine his heart.
And maybe...
you need to examine yours.
Because Christianity is not merely about keeping your hands technically clean while allowing hatred to rot your soul.
Jesus came for the whole person.
Hands.
Mind.
Conscience.
Memories.
Anger.
Trauma.
Hatred.
Guilt.
Everything.
And perhaps someone reading this has carried something for years that almost nobody knows about.
You pulled the trigger.
You survived.
Someone else didn't.
People called you brave.
They shook your hand.
They thanked you for your service.
They told you that you did what you had to do.
But sometimes, late at night...
you still see a face.
Maybe you keep wondering whether God sees you differently now.
Maybe you have whispered prayers that sounded more like questions.
“Jesus... can You still want me?”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people managed to keep themselves clean enough for God.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners could not rescue themselves...
so God came for them.
Jesus Christ stepped into our violent world.
He was betrayed.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Humiliated.
And crucified.
Yet while men were killing Him, Christ was not overcome by their hatred.
At the cross, the innocent Son of God bore sin so that guilty people could be reconciled to God.
And here is the scandal.
The murderer can come.
The soldier can come.
The police officer can come.
The criminal can come.
The pacifist can come.
The angry father can come.
The bitter mother can come.
The veteran haunted by memories can come.
The person who has never touched a gun but has murdered someone ten thousand times inside his imagination can come.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because the blood of Jesus does.
Repentance does not mean pretending evil was acceptable.
Grace does not rename darkness “light.”
Forgiveness does not mean God shrugs at sin.
At Calvary, God shows us simultaneously how seriously He takes sin...
and how deeply He loves sinners.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And the risen Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Think about Saul of Tarsus.
Before Christians called him Paul the apostle, believers knew him as the man coming for them.
Acts tells us that when Stephen was murdered, Saul approved of his death.
Imagine carrying that memory.
Stephen's face.
The stones.
The screams.
The coats at Saul's feet.
And then...
Jesus.
One encounter with the risen Christ did not rewrite history by pretending Saul's past never happened.
Jesus rewrote Saul.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The destroyer became a brother.
The man associated with death became a messenger announcing eternal life.
That is grace.
Not God pretending the scandal never happened.
God taking a sinner whose story looked irredeemable and writing something no one else could have imagined.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So what about the Christian police officer?
Serve Christ while you serve people.
Protect rather than dominate.
Tell the truth.
Refuse corruption.
Do not abuse frightened people merely because you possess authority over them.
Remember that the person in handcuffs still bears human dignity.
Use only the force genuinely necessary and lawful to protect life and uphold justice.
And if you ever face the terrible moment when lethal force appears necessary to protect innocent life, do not treat that moment casually.
A Christian should never love killing.
The goal is not destruction for destruction's sake.
The goal is protection.
Restraint.
Justice.
The preservation of innocent life.
And afterward, if your conscience is wounded, do not bury yourself underneath silence.
Bring everything into the light before Christ.
Seek wise pastoral care and appropriate professional support when trauma follows violence. Asking for help is not spiritual failure.
And Christian soldier...
your allegiance to Christ follows you onto the battlefield.
You do not receive permission to hate civilians.
You do not receive permission to torture.
You do not receive permission to rape, loot, execute the helpless, deliberately target innocent people, or obey manifestly evil orders.
The fact that another human being wears an enemy uniform does not erase the image-bearing humanity God gave him.
If force becomes necessary, there remains a profound moral difference between stopping a threat and loving the destruction of another human being.
John's words to soldiers still echo:
Do not exploit your power.
Do not falsely accuse.
Do not use your position for selfish gain.
But perhaps the deepest question is not:
“Can a Christian carry a gun?”
Perhaps it is:
“Can Christ trust my heart when I carry one?”
Can He trust you with authority?
Can He trust you when nobody is recording?
Can He trust you when anger surges through your body?
Can He trust you when someone insults you?
Can He trust you when vengeance feels easier than restraint?
Can He trust you to remember that justice belongs under God's authority and never under the control of your ego?
And civilian Christian...
Your weapon might simply look different.
Your weapon might be your tongue.
Your Facebook account.
Your gossip.
Your resentment.
Your ability to humiliate somebody publicly.
Your refusal to forgive.
Your secret satisfaction when an enemy suffers.
Jesus did not merely come to stop your hands from murdering.
He came to resurrect your heart.
Maybe that is why you found this today.
Not so you could win another argument about whether Christians should become soldiers.
Maybe God is exposing something quieter.
Someone you hate.
Someone you haven't forgiven.
Someone whose downfall you secretly want.
Someone whose name changes your heartbeat.
Be honest.
Who came into your mind?
Don't run from that answer.
Bring it to Jesus.
Forgiveness does not necessarily mean removing wise boundaries, abandoning justice, restoring trust without repentance, or pretending abuse never happened.
It means refusing to make vengeance your god.
You can seek justice without worshiping revenge.
You can protect the innocent without becoming intoxicated with hatred.
You can confront evil without allowing evil to reproduce itself inside you.
That is the narrow road.
And nobody walks it perfectly.
Which is precisely why we need Christ.
Be human.
Be honest.
No explanation required.
Let believers who see those words pray instead of judge.
And if Christ has already brought you through violence, bitterness, hatred, guilt, or a season when you barely recognized yourself, tell somebody what Jesus did.
Your testimony may become another person's doorway back toward hope.

Not because every sentence is easy, but because one day someone may ask you, “Does ‘Thou shalt not kill’ mean a Christian can never be a police officer or soldier?” and you will want more than a four-word answer.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to Christ, repent, heal, or grow deeper in the Word, you can also help this ministry keep putting Christ-centered biblical teaching in front of people who desperately need it.
Supporting Gospel work should never be presented as though paying money earns God's favor. It doesn't.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot buy God's blessing.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with your resources, one legitimate expression of Christian stewardship is voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel work that is helping people hear biblical truth. Another is sharing that truth freely so someone else can encounter it.
But the deeper reason to stay close is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
But before you leave, remember the officer standing in that doorway.
Remember the soldier staring into the darkness.
Remember the veteran awake at 2:17 in the morning.
Remember Saul standing beside the coats while Stephen died.
And remember the Savior hanging between criminals while violent men drove nails through His hands.
Human beings know how to write stories in blood.
Jesus knows how to take blood-stained stories and redeem the people inside them.
Maybe you have carried a weapon.
Maybe you have carried hatred.
Maybe you have carried guilt.
Maybe nobody knows.
Christ does.
And the same Jesus who commands us to turn from sin is the Jesus whose scarred hands remain open to repentant sinners.
Come to Him.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Now.
Because the greatest question is not whether your hands have ever held a weapon.
It is whether your life is now held by Christ.
The world may remember the worst chapter you ever lived—but Jesus is still holding the pen.
